title: Testing workflows

story: You change how Nova waits for a plan decision: the reminder now goes to Slack and to Jira. Before you merge, you want proof that the rest still works. A plan nobody decides on must be reminded once after a day and parked after three days, and a quick approval must start the work with no reminder at all.

But the real test of "parked after three days" takes three days, and it would post to the real Slack and the real Jira. And there is a second worry from last week: a deploy that added one step broke twelve open runs, and nobody noticed until a person pressed Approve.
hook.question: How do you test a workflow that waits for days and talks to Jira and Slack in a few seconds, and prove that a change will not break runs that are already open?

read.h: A test server that skips time
p: The testing package of the SDK can start a small Temporal server just for your tests, with TestWorkflowEnvironment.createTimeSkipping(). It is a real Temporal server, with one difference: whenever every workflow in it is only waiting for a timer, it moves its clock straight to the next timer instead of waiting. A three-day wait with nothing to do in between therefore takes milliseconds. The first time it runs, it downloads the test server, so it needs the internet once.

The test itself looks like the code you already know. You start a worker on the test server's connection with Worker.create, run the workflow with execute, which starts it and waits for its result, and check the result. worker.runUntil runs the worker exactly as long as the promise you give it, and then shuts it down cleanly.

notes.text: One test server for the whole file. Starting it takes a second or two, so do not start one per test.
Fake activities: plain functions that write down what the real ones would post.
runUntil: the worker runs until the workflow's result is ready, then stops.
Three days passed in about a second: one day to the reminder, two more to parking.

read.see:
$ node --test
ok 1 - a plan nobody decides on is reminded once, then parked
ok 2 - an approval on the first day starts the work, with no reminder
# pass 2
# fail 0
# duration_ms 2020.951

p: The test does not check Slack or Jira. It checks the workflow's decisions: when to remind, when to park, what to do after an approval. That is possible because activities are only functions handed to the worker. In production the worker gets the real ones; in a test it gets fakes that record what they were asked to do, and the workflow cannot tell the difference. The usual name for these fakes is mocks.

A test can also play a person. The test below uses fakeActivities, a small helper that returns the same two fakes as before together with their posted list. It sends the decidePlan signal through the run's handle, exactly as the Slack app would, and then checks that only the first message was posted. When you need to stop between two timers, env.sleep moves the test clock forward by an amount you choose, for example 25 hours, so you can approve on the second day and check that exactly one reminder went out.

notes.text: start returns a handle at once, so the test can act while the run waits.
The test plays the requester pressing Approve.
The decision was quick, so the fake Slack got one message and no reminder.

deeper.h: Go deeper: testing a crash or a lost VM
p: Failures are just as easy to fake. A fake workInSandbox can throw SandboxDead on its first call, the way the real one does after five minutes without a heartbeat from the VM, and return a PR on the second call. The test then checks what the workflow did about it: it claimed a second VM and finished. A second test makes it fail twice and checks that the run stops and asks for a person.

A worker crash between two steps is tested by running the first half with one worker, stopping it, and finishing with a new worker. The new worker has nothing in memory, so it must replay, and the test proves the replay works.

read.h: Replay tests: old histories, new code
p: The second worry was the deploy that broke twelve open runs. A replay test finds that kind of change before it is merged. You save the history of a real run as JSON with temporal workflow show --output json, and the test feeds each saved history to Worker.runReplayHistory together with the current workflow code. The worker replays the history, exactly as it would in production after a deploy, and if the code asks for different steps than the history recorded, the test fails with DeterminismViolationError.

Keep one saved history for each path that matters: a plan approved at once, a plan changed, a question answered, a VM lost, a ticket parked. Add one whenever you add a path. In the lab you make an unpatched change and watch this test fail, then wrap the change in patched and watch it pass.

notes.text: test/histories/*.json: one file per saved run, made with temporal workflow show --output json.
Replays the whole history with today's code, with no server and no activities. A mismatch throws.

lab.title: Test three days in two seconds
needs: The p7-1 lab folder, for worker.mjs and start.mjs
Internet once, to download the test server
lab.goal: Test a workflow's three-day wait in seconds with a time-skipping server and fake activities, and add a replay test that catches a change that would break open runs.

guess.q: The workflow waits up to 1 day, sends a reminder, and waits 2 more days before it parks. In the time-skipping test server, with fake activities and no signal, how long does the test take?

options.text: About 3 days, because the timers are real Temporal timers.
options.why: They are real timers, but the test server moves its clock to the next timer whenever nothing else is happening.

options.text: A second or two, because the server jumps to each timer when every workflow is only waiting.
options.why: That is time skipping. Most of the time is spent starting the server and bundling the workflow.

options.text: It never ends, because nobody sends the decidePlan signal.
options.why: Both waits have a timeout. When the timers fire, condition returns false, and the run parks itself.

follow.say: Make the lab folder and install the packages, this time with the testing package. The last one, protobufjs@8.8.1, makes all Temporal packages share one copy of that library; with two copies, reading a saved history fails with TypeError: type must be a Type.
follow.do:
mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/p7-7 && cd ~/academy-labs/p7-7
npm init -y > /dev/null && npm pkg set type=module
npm install @temporalio/client@1.24.0 @temporalio/worker@1.24.0 @temporalio/workflow@1.24.0 @temporalio/testing@1.24.0 protobufjs@8.8.1
follow.see: added 149 packages, and audited 150 packages in 11s

follow.say: Write the workflow to test: the plan wait from the signals lab, but with the real times, one day and two days.
Write the tests: one time-skipping server for the file, fake activities that record what they would post, and two tests.
Run them. The first run downloads the test server, so it takes a little longer; after that, three days of waiting take about two seconds.
follow.see:
ok 1 - a plan nobody decides on is reminded once, then parked
ok 2 - an approval on the first day starts the work, with no reminder
# pass 2
# fail 0

follow.say: Now the replay test needs a real history. Start the dev server in a second tab, and in this tab write two activities that print, and borrow the worker and the client from p7-1.
follow.do:
# second tab
temporal server start-dev

# this tab
cat > activities.mjs <<'EOF'
export const notify = async (text) => console.log(`[slack] ${text}`);
export const parkTicket = async (ticket) => console.log(`[jira] parked ${ticket}`);
EOF
cp ../p7-1/worker.mjs ../p7-1/start.mjs .

follow.say: Start the worker in a third tab, then run and approve one ticket, and save its history as JSON.
follow.do:
# third tab
cd ~/academy-labs/p7-7 && node worker.mjs

# this tab
node start.mjs
temporal workflow signal -w nova:RH-1234 --name decidePlan --input '{"kind":"approve","by":"sean"}'
mkdir -p histories && temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1234 --output json > histories/approved.json
head -c 120 histories/approved.json

lab.build: Write a third test, "an approval on the second day comes after exactly one reminder". Start the run, move the test clock forward by 25 hours with env.sleep, then send the approval and check that the result is "approve by sean" and that exactly two messages were posted: the plan and one reminder. The workflow now calls checkReadiness on new runs, so add a fake for it to fakeActivities too. Then run every test file at once with node --test.
checks: node --test ticket-to-pr.test.mjs shows ok 1 and ok 2, and the whole file takes a few seconds, not three days.
histories/approved.json starts with { "events": [ and the replay test passed before your change.
The careless change made the replay test fail with DeterminismViolationError and the words Nondeterminism error.
With patched around the new call, the replay test passes again.
For your build: node --test runs every test file and shows # pass 4 and # fail 0.
lab.fix: A teammate added checkReadiness to the workflow, patched it correctly, and pushed. CI never finished: the test job ran until it was killed, and its log was thousands of lines of Activity function checkReadiness is not registered on this Worker, available activities: ["notify","parkTicket"], with the attempt number going up and up. Remove checkReadiness from your fakeActivities and run node --test ticket-to-pr.test.mjs to see it (stop it with Ctrl+C). Why does the test hang instead of failing, and what is the one-line fix?
explain: Why does a three-day wait take about a second in the test server, and when would it not skip?
Your tests use fake activities. What do they prove about the workflow, and what do they not prove?
What does the replay test catch that the time-skipping tests cannot?
lab.done: Your time-skipping tests pass in seconds, the replay test failed on an unpatched change and passed once it was patched, and you stopped the worker and the dev server.

check.q: A workflow waits for condition(..., "3 days") and nothing else happens. What does the time-skipping test server do?

options.text: It waits three real days, because a timer cannot be skipped
options.why: Skipping timers is exactly what this server is for.

options.text: It moves its clock to the moment the timer fires, so the test continues at once
options.why: When every workflow is only waiting for a timer, nothing can happen before it fires, so the server jumps there.

options.text: It fires the timer at once and also skips the activities after it
options.why: Only waiting is skipped. Activities after the timer run normally, on your fake functions.

check.q: Why does the test pass fake activities to the worker instead of the real ones?

options.text: Real activities cannot run inside a test
options.why: They could, but they would post to the real Slack and Jira, and the test would depend on those services.

options.text: The test checks the workflow's decisions, and fakes let it record what would be posted without touching Jira or Slack
options.why: Activities are plain functions handed to the worker, so a test can hand it fakes that write down every call.

options.text: The time-skipping server refuses network calls
options.why: It does not. Fakes are a choice, to keep the test fast and focused on the workflow.

check.q: Your change passes every time-skipping test but fails the replay test with DeterminismViolationError. What does that mean?

options.text: The test is flaky; run it again
options.why: Replay is exact. The same history and the same code fail the same way every time.

options.text: The saved history is out of date and should be replaced with a new one
options.why: That hides the problem. Open runs in production have exactly those old histories.

options.text: New runs work, but runs that started on the old code would break after the deploy, so the change needs patched
options.why: The time-skipping tests start fresh runs. The replay test checks old histories, which is what open runs are.

p: The orchestrator's tests use the time-skipping environment and fake activities for every path of ticketToPr: approve, change, reject, a question and its answer, a worker crash between steps, a lost VM and two lost VMs. The fan-out rules have their own: two starts for one ticket give one run, a fourth Nova ticket waits for a slot, and the kill switch stops a run between steps.

A replay test runs on every pull request: orchestrator/test/replay.test.ts replays every saved history in test/histories with the new code. Together with the patching rule, it is what makes it safe to deploy the orchestrator while runs are days into their life.

tickets.why: ticketToPr's tests with TestWorkflowEnvironment.createTimeSkipping() and fake activities.
The replay test in CI, run against saved histories on every PR.
The lost-VM tests: one lost VM is replaced, a second one stops the run.
Fan-out tests: one run per ticket, slots that make work wait, and the kill switch.

words.plain: A test Temporal server that jumps its clock to the next timer when every workflow is only waiting.
A plain function given to the test worker instead of the real activity, often recording how it was called.
Moves the test server's clock forward by a chosen amount, so a test can act between two timers.
A test that replays saved histories with the current workflow code, to catch changes that would break open runs.
The error a replay throws when the code asks for different steps than the history recorded.

review.q: Write the shape of a time-skipping test from memory: setup, worker, run, assertion.
review.a: before: env = await TestWorkflowEnvironment.createTimeSkipping(); in the test: Worker.create with env.nativeConnection, a task queue, workflowsPath and fake activities; worker.runUntil(env.client.workflow.execute(...)); assert on the result and on what the fakes recorded; after: env.teardown().

review.q: Which paths of ticketToPr deserve a saved history in test/histories, and when do you add one?
review.a: Every path that matters: approved at once, changed, a question answered, a VM lost, parked. Add one whenever a change adds a new path.

review.q: A test hangs and logs "Activity function ... is not registered on this Worker". What happened?
review.a: The workflow calls an activity that the test's fakes do not include. The activity fails and is retried forever, very fast in the time-skipping server. Add a fake for it.

remember: Test the workflow's decisions in a time-skipping server with fake activities, and replay saved histories so a change cannot break the runs that are already open.
